claims.text: The authors provide carbonbenchmark, combining CodeCarbon measurements with fitted training curves, and demonstrate it on three small tasks using an RTX 4060 Ti over a one-hour training period.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors propose SMAJ as a cost-aware model-selection concept and recommend reporting research emissions; the paper does not establish a generally validated equivalence or noninferiority procedure for selecting the smallest adequate model.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The reported review of 5,285 NeurIPS 2025 papers classifies papers with LLMs after a 200-paper model-agreement study; its corpus estimates are automated classifications, not a human-adjudicated census.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent validation on frontier-scale training or inference workloads.

importance_rationale: If its measurement proposals prove reliable at larger scales, they could make energy and carbon costs visible in AI research and model selection. Current experiments are small and several inference inputs are assumptions, so this is a methods proposal rather than a validated standard.
limitations: Training examples cover only three small tasks and one local GPU; they do not establish frontier-scale measurement accuracy.
The NeurIPS paper-use estimates rely on automated classification rather than human adjudication.
Proprietary inference emissions use assumed active parameter counts and generic hardware/grid factors, not measured per-model energy.
SMAJ’s uncertainty threshold is not a demonstrated equivalence design and may require selection-bias control.
summary: The authors introduce carbonbenchmark, which combines CodeCarbon measurements with fitted training curves, and propose a “Smallest Model that Achieves the Job” (SMAJ) selection approach. They report illustrative fits on Fashion-MNIST, GLUE SST-2 and UCI Adult, and an automated review of 5,285 NeurIPS 2025 papers using LLM classification. Their proprietary-inference emissions examples use assumed active parameter counts and generic hardware/grid factors; these are estimates, not measured model-specific emissions. The paper argues for reporting research emissions and treating environmental cost alongside accuracy.

technical.claimed_result: Authors recommend reporting study emissions and propose training-curve and smallest-adequate-model metrics.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary paper describes its tool, methods and illustrative experiments; the research desk did not independently run the code or validate emissions estimates.
technical.mechanism: Measures local training emissions and fits exponential, delayed-exponential and power-law learning curves; proposes a single-parameter training-efficiency measure and SMAJ selection framing.
technical.regime: Illustrations on Fashion-MNIST, GLUE SST-2 and UCI Adult, local RTX 4060 Ti training, plus an automated review of 5,285 NeurIPS 2025 papers.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper discusses accuracy-focused state-of-the-art selection and common learning-curve forms; no validated environmental benchmark baseline is established.

title: A paper proposes carbon reporting and a smallest-model selection rule for AI research
why_it_matters: Environmental measurement choices can affect comparisons of model quality and compute cost. This paper offers methods and a reporting proposal, but its small training examples and assumed frontier-inference inputs do not establish reliable footprint estimates or a validated model-selection standard.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors compare 33 judge configurations with 4,501 held-out worker ratings from 307 occupations and report above-chance tie-aware ranking for all configurations.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Reported judge acceptance shares range from 3.0% to 97.9%, compared with 61.1% in the sampled worker ratings; these are corpus-relative agreement results, not employment or productivity estimates.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a prespecified validation contrast within one two-epoch fine-tuned lineage, a bundled few-shot/listwise protocol improves ordering while reducing task- and occupation-level agreement.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or validation on multi-rated, employment-weighted occupational data.

importance_rationale: If similar judge-scale mismatches occur in broader occupational measurement, estimates derived from AI task benchmarks could change materially. This study is an audit of one sampled US English rating corpus, not a measure of workplace productivity or employment effects.
limitations: Each response has one worker rating; sampled worker judgments are not noise-free ground truth.
Occupation-level split-half reliability is low; the source reports 0.093.
The US English text corpus is not employment-weighted; occupations and response-generator variants overlap across splits.
Most test comparisons were exploratory after repeated inspection; the prespecified protocol contrast bundles several changes.
No real workplace output, productivity, hiring or employment effect is measured.
summary: The authors evaluate 33 LLM-judge configurations against 4,501 held-out worker ratings spanning 307 occupations in a US English text corpus. They report above-chance tie-aware response ranking for all configurations, while predicted acceptance shares range from 3.0% to 97.9% against the sampled workers’ 61.1%. A prespecified validation contrast within one fine-tuned lineage reports that a bundled few-shot/listwise protocol improves ordering while reducing task- and occupation-level agreement. The study audits agreement with sampled worker ratings; it does not measure objective work quality, AI productivity or employment effects.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report that ranking agreement can coexist with large mismatches in score levels and occupation aggregates.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary paper specifies the corpus, splits and judge configurations; the research desk did not independently reproduce its analysis.
technical.mechanism: Compares pointwise and listwise judge configurations with worker ratings at response-ranking, score-calibration, acceptance-share and occupation-aggregate levels.
technical.regime: 4,501 held-out ratings from 307 occupations in one US English text corpus; 33 existing judge configurations across six model families.
technical.strongest_baseline: Sampled worker ratings provide the study’s reference, with acknowledged low reliability at occupation level; they are not objective ground truth.

title: An occupational audit finds LLM judges rank responses better than they match worker score levels
why_it_matters: Occupational AI assessments can change when judge scores are converted into acceptance shares or occupation-level estimates. The paper shows that response ordering and score-level agreement are distinct measurement targets in one corpus, while leaving worker-reference reliability and transfer to real workplace outcomes unresolved.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors evaluated 66 model–harness configurations across TUA-Bench, ALE-CLI and a 63-task non-H100 Terminal-Bench 4 subset, and report that model rankings vary by harness and task collection.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On the paper’s Terminal-Bench 4 subset, Claude leads GPT-6 Astra by 7.94 points under OpenHands but trails by 30.16 points under PI; GPT-6 Astra scores 60.32% at $4.66 per task with PI and 52.38% at $19.94 with DeepSeek Harness.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper releases adapters, evaluation code and 6,204 scored task trajectories, enabling artifact inspection but not independently validating the reported outcomes or billing.

evidence_gaps.description: Independent matched multi-run reproduction and ranking uncertainty are unavailable.
The paper uses harness-specific defaults and high-effort labels that may not imply equal reasoning budgets.

importance_rationale: If the measured model–harness interactions generalize, they can change agent system selection and the work delivered per API dollar across common task settings. The study spans 66 configurations and three benchmarks, but one counted run per task and differing harness defaults leave causal attribution and transfer uncertain.
limitations: Results are author-reported; the research desk did not independently rerun the benchmarks or validate provider invoices.
Each task contributes one counted run after reruns; no run-to-run variance or ranking stability is established.
Harness context management, retries, compaction, turn limits and effective reasoning budgets differ; this is not a matched intervention isolating harness causality.
The task subsets and reward conventions are local to this campaign and are not direct reproductions of upstream leaderboard results.
summary: Li et al. report 66 model–harness configurations across TUA-Bench, ALE-CLI and a 63-task non-H100 subset of Terminal-Bench 4. Rankings reverse by harness: on the paper’s Terminal-Bench subset, Claude leads GPT-6 Astra by 7.94 points under OpenHands but trails by 30.16 points under PI. GPT-6 Astra scores 60.32% at $4.66 per task under PI versus 52.38% at $19.94 under DeepSeek Harness. The authors release adapters, evaluation code and 6,204 scored trajectories. These are author-reported results from one counted run per task; harness defaults and effective reasoning budgets differ, so the comparison does not isolate a causal harness effect or establish ranking stability.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report model ranking reversals across harnesses, task-dependent best harnesses and substantial differences in task score and API cost for the same model.
technical.compute_or_cost: Author-reported OpenRouter API cost per task, including harness auxiliary model calls and excluding evaluator calls.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary paper and its public artifact links exist; the research desk verified the paper text and the reported results table but did not reproduce the experiment.
technical.implementation_status: Research preprint with public adapters, evaluation code and scored trajectories; independent reproduction not performed.
technical.mechanism: Crosses five models with four configurable harnesses on three task collections, adding Codex–GPT and Claude Code–Claude native references; compares reward, reported cost and selected trajectories.
technical.regime: 66 configurations on TUA-Bench (120 tasks), ALE-CLI (99 tasks) and a 63-task non-H100 Terminal-Bench 4 subset; one counted run per task after reruns.
technical.reproducibility: Public artifacts are linked by the paper; revisions and independent matched multi-run results still need to be frozen and checked.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within-paper matched task identifiers compare harnesses for a given model; the comparison does not equalize all harness defaults or reasoning budgets.

title: A 66-configuration study reports model–harness ranking reversals across agent tasks
why_it_matters: The reported reversals show that model-only rankings may not predict the performance or API cost of a deployed agent configuration. The result supports evaluating model, harness and intended task together, while leaving matched-budget causal effects and repeated-run uncertainty unresolved.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors analyze 590 harness-triggered compaction boundaries from 275 trajectories on 147 AppWorld tasks using paired replay before and after compaction, one minimax-m3 agent/compressor and a 4,096-token context.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The prespecified contrast between prior-write and read-only histories is a wide null, while the naive “has written” label mostly tracks trajectory phase.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The best reported history trigger has held-out AUROC 0.66 versus a same-boundary replicate yardstick of 0.72; a frozen two-feature trigger avoids 20.6% of positive-burden boundaries at 83.7% retention by count, but has no detected burden-mass advantage.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION_OF_SOURCE
claims.text: The study does not establish cross-model generality, a deployable compaction policy, or performance against a token-budget rule at matched retention.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or test across different models, compressors or harnesses was performed.
The public observables omit ordered histories, token counts, compression ratio and summary text; matched-retention comparison to token-budget compaction is unavailable.

importance_rationale: If replicated across agent harnesses, per-boundary prediction of compaction harm could change context-management policies and evaluation design for long-horizon agents. The consequence is meaningful but bounded: this paper reports weak signals in one model/compressor and one AppWorld cohort, with no demonstrated deployable trigger or cross-system transfer.
limitations: All performance figures are author-reported; the research desk did not independently reproduce the analysis.
The cohort contains one agent model, one compressor and one deliberately tight 4,096-token window, with harness-triggered boundaries only on AppWorld.
Each boundary uses three to five replays per arm and the paired harm outcome is noisy; the same-boundary replicate AUROC is 0.72 while three-class sign agreement is 0.55 (κ=0.28).
The public release omits ordered actions, token counts, compression ratio and summary text, preventing a matched-retention comparison with a token-budget policy.
The source reports no data redistribution permission and the cited repository revision had no license file; independent replication must use authorized data access and must not rehost the corpus.
Trigger frontiers are offline plug-in estimates over logged outcomes, not a deployable fitted policy or measured task-success/latency benefit.
summary: Pakhomov and Nijkamp use TRACE’s paired-replay corpus to test whether an agent’s pre-compaction history predicts the harm caused by summarizing that context. Across 590 harness-triggered boundaries from 275 trajectories on 147 AppWorld tasks, the prespecified contrast between histories with and without prior writes is a wide null (dU@3 −0.062; 95% interval −0.209 to +0.079); a naive “has written” label largely tracks trajectory phase. The best history-based trigger reaches held-out AUROC 0.66, below a same-boundary replay yardstick of 0.72. A frozen two-feature logistic trigger at 83.7% retention avoids 20.6% of positive-burden boundaries by count, but has no detected advantage on burden mass. The study does not establish a deployable compaction policy: it covers one agent/compressor, one AppWorld cohort and a 4,096-token window, and cannot compare with a token-budget rule at matched retention.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report a wide null on the prespecified prior-write versus read-only dU@3 contrast (−0.062; 95% interval −0.209 to +0.079), and find the naive “has written” label mostly tracks trajectory phase. The best history-based trigger reaches held-out AUROC 0.66 [0.61, 0.70], compared with 0.72 [0.69, 0.75] for a same-boundary replicate yardstick. At 83.7% retained compaction opportunities, a frozen two-feature logistic trigger avoids 20.6% [15.6%, 25.6%] of positive-burden boundaries by count but shows no advantage on burden mass (−0.001 [−0.034, +0.035]). These estimates are paper-reported and partly post hoc.
technical.compute_or_cost: No operational cost, token savings, latency, task-completion advantage or matched-retention comparison against a token-budget policy is measured.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public preprint specifies a paired replay over 590 harness-triggered boundaries from 275 trajectories on 147 AppWorld tasks, using one minimax-m3 agent/compressor and a 4,096-token window. the research desk has not independently reproduced the analysis; performance results below are author-reported.
technical.implementation_status: Research preprint arXiv v1 dated 2026-10-06. No deployable trigger or production result is established.
technical.mechanism: At each TRACE compaction boundary, the authors replay the same task prefix under the full pre-compaction context and under the stored summary plus retained turn, then compare the next one to five actions. They score blocked calls, repeated/refetched calls and their union, and train history-based triggers to select boundaries where compaction should be deferred.
technical.novelty: Uses paired counterfactual replays at individual context-compaction boundaries to evaluate next-action process harm, then compares history-based timing triggers against both a random-rule expectation and a same-boundary reproducibility yardstick.
technical.regime: One harness-triggered context-compaction corpus: 590 boundaries from 275 of 294 trajectories on 147 AppWorld tasks; one minimax-m3 agent/compressor, 4,096-token context, three to five replays per arm/boundary and a next-action burden outcome. Agent-chosen compaction, other models/compressors and non-AppWorld tasks are outside scope.
technical.reproducibility: The paper documents the analysis and identifies a public TRACE repository revision, but says the underlying data cannot be redistributed and the repository had no license file. The analysis record is available on request; the research desk did not obtain or reproduce it.
technical.strongest_baseline: A same-boundary split-half replay is used as a noise/replicability yardstick, not a deployable policy. The trigger is compared with a uniform random-rule expectation at equal-weight compaction opportunities; the paper cannot evaluate a token-budget rule at matched retention because token counts are not released.

title: A paired-replay study finds weak history signals for predicting when agent context compaction will hurt
why_it_matters: Context compaction is often triggered by a global token threshold, but delaying it based on recent agent behavior only helps if the history predicts which boundaries will be harmed. This study reports weak prediction in one controlled corpus and shows that a simple “has written” signal can be confounded with trajectory phase. It gives agent-harness designers a counterfactual evaluation target, while leaving cross-model generality and matched-retention policy value unresolved.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Six national cybersecurity agencies published joint guidance on agentic AI security on 2026-05-01; the document is aimed at government, critical-infrastructure and industry stakeholders and is nonbinding guidance.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The guidance recommends distinct cryptographically anchored agent identities, mutual TLS for agent/API calls, trusted registries and least-privilege permissions.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The guidance recommends role-bounded delegation with expiry and recorded grant chains, risk-based human approval for high-impact actions, and continuous runtime identity and authorization checks through a central policy decision point for each action.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The guidance does not report jurisdictional adoption, conformity audits, independent attack tests or measured reduction in security incidents.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent implementation audit or controlled attack evaluation of the recommended identity, delegation-expiry and per-action authorization controls was inspected.
No jurisdictional adoption, procurement requirement or conformity assessment was established.

importance_rationale: If followed in government, critical infrastructure or enterprise systems, the joint recommendations could shape identity, privilege, delegation and runtime authorization controls for agentic AI. Their decision value is meaningful, but the guidance is nonbinding and the agencies provide no adoption, audit or measured outcome evidence.
limitations: The guidance is advisory and does not impose a legal or procurement duty.
No evidence of government or industry adoption, implementation conformity, independent red-team results or measured attack reduction was inspected.
The document recommends a broad control set but does not establish which measures are most effective or how they trade off against cost, usability or agent task performance.
organizations: New Zealand National Cyber Security Centre
United Kingdom National Cyber Security Centre
summary: On 2026-05-01, cybersecurity agencies from Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States published joint nonbinding guidance for LLM-based agentic AI systems. The 29-page document recommends distinct cryptographically anchored identities for agents, mutual TLS for agent/API calls, least-privilege permissions, trusted registries, controlled delegation with expiry and recorded grant chains, risk-based human approval, and continuous identity and authorization checks through a central policy decision point for each action. It also calls for threat-modelled evaluations, red-teaming, monitoring and staged deployment. These are recommendations, not a binding rule or evidence that any government has adopted the controls or that they measurably reduce attacks.

technical.claimed_result: The authoring agencies present these controls as practical security recommendations. The document reports no measured reduction in attacks, adoption or conformity results.
technical.compute_or_cost: No implementation cost, security incident reduction or operational overhead is measured.
technical.demonstrated_result: The official 29-page joint guidance explicitly recommends a unique cryptographically anchored identity for each agent, mutual TLS for inter-agent and agent-to-service calls, trusted registries and least privilege; role boundaries with delegation expiry and recorded grant chains; risk-based multi-agent/human approvals; and continuous runtime identity and authorization verification through a central policy decision point for each action.
technical.implementation_status: Public joint guidance published May 1, 2026. No binding adoption, procurement mandate, conformity assessment or implementation outcome was established in this check.
technical.mechanism: Six national cybersecurity agencies provide lifecycle recommendations for securing LLM-based agentic AI systems, organized around design, development, deployment and operation. Controls cover identity, privilege, input/tool integrity, evaluation, human oversight and runtime monitoring.
technical.novelty: A multi-agency baseline that makes identity-based boundaries, delegation expiry/grant-chain recording and centralized per-action authorization explicit controls for agentic systems, alongside conventional cyber safeguards.
technical.regime: Nonbinding guidance for government, critical-infrastructure and industry stakeholders deploying LLM-based agentic AI systems; it addresses the system lifecycle and both risks to agents and risks from agent behaviour.
technical.reproducibility: The official guidance document is publicly accessible. Its recommendations can be tested, but the document itself provides no controlled implementation or attack-evaluation results.
technical.strongest_baseline: The guidance references existing zero-trust, identity-management, secure-by-design and software supply-chain practices; its distinctive contribution is applying them to autonomous agents, tool use, delegation and per-action runtime authorization.

title: Six national cybersecurity agencies publish joint guidance for secure adoption of agentic AI
why_it_matters: The guidance turns broad least-privilege principles into a concrete, testable baseline for identity, delegation and per-action authorization in agentic systems. It is useful for procurement and security evaluations, but the agencies report no conformity data, adoption requirements, independent attack tests or measured security outcomes.

The notice’s statement that other requirements remain unchanged does not independently establish funding availability or implementation details.
summary: On 2026-09-30, Hubei’s Commerce Department issued an effective notice revising the province’s 2026 consumer-goods trade-in subsidy categories from 2026-10-01. The ten-category list now explicitly includes embodied service robots, cooking robots, exoskeletons, companion robots and robot dogs; it also reshapes smart cleaning and kitchen categories and adds cameras/drones, age-support products and smart furniture. The notice says other requirements remain unchanged. This establishes an official eligibility change, not consumer take-up, robot sales, subsidy outlays or incremental demand.

technical.claimed_result: No consumer uptake, subsidy redemption, sales, fiscal outlay or causal demand effect is reported in the notice.
technical.compute_or_cost: The reviewed notice gives no subsidy appropriation, spending, redemption count or product-price data.
technical.demonstrated_result: The official Chinese notice lists ten categories and expressly includes embodied service robots, cooking robots, exoskeleton robots, companion robots/robot dogs, digital cameras/drones, age-support products and smart furniture. It replaces the prior category wording and is marked effective.
technical.implementation_status: Official provincial notice is marked effective; revised categories took effect October 1, 2026. Consumer eligibility at individual-SKU level, uptake and program spending are unverified.
technical.mechanism: Hubei’s Commerce Department revised the eligible categories in its 2026 consumer-goods trade-in subsidy program. The notice states the revised categories take effect on 2026-10-01 and that other requirements remain unchanged.
technical.novelty: A provincial implementation change explicitly names several embodied and service robot types in a consumer subsidy basket, creating a trackable policy-to-purchase channel rather than a general AI strategy statement.
technical.regime: Hubei Province’s 2026 consumer-goods trade-in subsidy category list, revised September 30 and effective October 1, 2026. Product-level eligibility and implementation data are not specified in the reviewed notice.
technical.reproducibility: The official notice is publicly accessible. No implementation ledger, qualifying SKU list or post-effective-date outcome data was inspected.
technical.strongest_baseline: Hubei Commerce Department notice 鄂商务发〔2026〕17号, whose earlier ten-category list is reproduced in the September 30 revision; the new notice says all other requirements remain unchanged.

title: Hubei expands its 2026 consumer subsidy basket to include embodied, cooking, exoskeleton and companion robots
why_it_matters: The revision turns several robot types into explicitly eligible consumer categories under a provincial subsidy program, creating a concrete policy channel that could affect purchase prices and demand. Its actual reach depends on qualifying product definitions, consumer redemptions and program funding; the notice alone does not establish take-up or economic impact.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Under the authors’ shared 1e-6 learning-rate, 104-step setup, the reported GRPO gain over base rises from +0.001 at 2.3B to +0.078 at 31B; the 2.3B result is not significant and each size has one training run.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: At early checkpoints, the authors report that tripling the learning rate improves the seller score over the shared-rate checkpoint at every tested size; after 104 shared-rate steps the difference is not detectable at 12B and 31B.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The observed size pattern does not isolate parameter-count effects because architecture changes between the 4.5B E-series and 12B conventional checkpoints, compute is not FLOP-matched, and there is one training seed per arm.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that the 10×-rate 2.3B arm’s pooled reward gain concentrates on the evaluation buyer from the training buyer’s model family and is accompanied by frequent JSON-fragment leakage into buyer-visible prose.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION_OF_SOURCE
claims.text: The study does not demonstrate commercial negotiation transfer, throughput, energy use, or serving-cost advantage.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent multi-seed reproduction across model sizes and buyer families.
Transfer from the synthetic bilateral task to live procurement, marketplaces, or multi-party negotiation is untested.
Authors did not report metered training FLOPs/GPU-hours or serving throughput, latency, energy, and cost.

importance_rationale: If repeatable in comparable bargaining regimes, the result changes local choices about learning-rate tuning and evaluation design for small negotiation agents. Its field consequence is bounded by one model family, one seed per arm, architecture/compute confounds, two held-out buyers, and no measured operational cost or live transfer.
limitations: All performance numbers are author-reported and not independently reproduced by the research desk.
Each size/rate arm is trained once; scenario bootstrap intervals do not estimate training-run variance.
Model size and architecture co-vary between the E-series 2.3B/4.5B checkpoints and conventional 12B/31B checkpoints; matched steps are not matched FLOPs.
Evaluation uses two held-out buyer models, only one outside the training buyers’ model family, and one underpowered held-out domain.
The task is a synthetic, bilateral, seller-side bargaining environment with a single issue schema; no live procurement, marketplace or customer outcome is measured.
Authors report no measured wall-clock GPU-hours, throughput, latency, energy or serving cost; no scripted baseline seller is included.
summary: Tabacof and Joglekar report a controlled GRPO study of four Gemma 4 seller checkpoints (2.3B–31B effective parameters) in bilateral multi-issue bargaining. With one shared 1e-6 learning rate and 104 steps, author-reported gains over each base checkpoint rise from +0.001 (95% interval −0.019 to +0.021; not significant) at 2.3B to +0.023 at 4.5B, +0.063 at 12B and +0.078 at 31B; each arm has one training run. At early checkpoints, a 3× learning rate improves over the shared rate at all sizes, while after 104 shared-rate steps the difference is not detectable at 12B or 31B. The study does not establish a scaling law: size and architecture co-vary, training is not FLOP-matched, and the authors report only two held-out buyers and one underpowered held-out domain. These are paper-reported results in one synthetic negotiation environment, not evidence of commercial transfer.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report 1,152 paired episodes per arm over nine domains and two held-out buyer models. At shared 1e-6 LR and 104 steps, the gains over base are +0.001 at 2.3B (95% interval −0.019 to +0.021; not significant), +0.023 at 4.5B, +0.063 at 12B and +0.078 at 31B, with one training seed per size. A 3× LR run read at step 56 improves over the shared-rate early checkpoint at each size; versus 104 shared-rate steps the difference is not detectable at 12B or 31B. The separate 10× LR 2.3B arm gains +0.050 pooled score over base, but the authors report that the gain concentrates on the GPT-family buyer and that 91.6% of its seller turns leaked JSON fragments into buyer-visible prose.
technical.compute_or_cost: At matched optimizer steps, authors estimate the 31B arm used 6–13× the 2.3B arm training FLOPs depending on parameter-count convention; no per-arm wall-clock GPU-hours were metered. For evaluation serving, 31B needed four 48 GB accelerators for a 16k context while smaller checkpoints fit on one. Throughput, latency, energy and serving cost were not benchmarked.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper and its reported evaluation tables are publicly accessible. the research desk has not independently reproduced the results; numeric outcomes below are author-reported claims.
technical.implementation_status: Research preprint (arXiv v1, 2026-10-05); accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on SLMs for Agentic Systems according to the arXiv record. No commercial deployment is established.
technical.mechanism: The authors train Gemma 4 seller policies with GRPO against a frozen GPT-5.5/GPT-5.4-mini buyer pool using a programmatic terminal reward based on seller utility, no-deal penalty, malformed-output penalty and episode length. They evaluate paired scenarios against two held-out buyer models.
technical.novelty: A shared-recipe comparison of RL gain across four Gemma 4 sizes on a strategic multi-agent task, with an explicit learning-rate comparison, paired scenario evaluation and diagnostics that expose opponent-family concentration and formatting degeneration.
technical.regime: A synthetic bilateral, multi-issue bargaining environment with 7–10 contract issues, frozen LLM buyers, up to 12 rounds, seller-side utility reward, four Gemma 4 checkpoints from 2.3B to 31B effective parameters, one training seed per arm, and two held-out buyer models across nine domains (one held-out domain has 128 episodes).
technical.reproducibility: The paper describes its reward, training and evaluation protocols in detail. No linked task-specific code/data artifact was found in this review; no independent multi-seed reproduction was performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within each size, the instruction-tuned Gemma 4 base model under the same evaluation configuration. The paper also compares with two frontier model sellers, but decoding and service differ; it includes no scripted seller baseline.

title: A controlled Gemma 4 study finds learning-rate-sensitive gains in small-model negotiation
why_it_matters: The study shows why post-training comparisons on agent tasks need tuned learning rates, multiple training seeds and adversarially varied counterparties: a fixed-rate size trend can mix model capacity, architecture, compute and optimization, while pooled reward can conceal buyer-family-specific behavior. Its bounded results give a useful design baseline for negotiation-agent evaluation, but they do not establish that smaller models can replace frontier systems in procurement or marketplaces.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Guidance-TTT updates a compact guidance model that proposes parent-conditioned strategic edits while a stronger GLM-5.2 executor remains frozen and implements complete candidate solutions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Authors report results on Polyomino Packing (91.89), Lasso (0.1739), AHC058 (850,082,731) and TriMul (1,129 μs), with heterogeneous task-specific baselines.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: A separate Polyomino configuration reports about 58% lower service cost when adapting 8B guidance rather than a 120B model, with scores 83.19 and 83.72; this does not establish general cost reduction.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Single trajectories, differing protocols and candidate implementation failures limit conclusions about general search productivity and cost.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent multi-seed reproduction under matched guidance controls and equal total candidate/API/GPU budget.
Full external run archives and hash-bound payloads were not fetched or verified, and full cost accounting against all baselines is incomplete.

importance_rationale: If the reported gains and reduced adaptation cost survive matched independent replication, training a compact model to propose strategic changes while a stronger executor remains fixed could improve the economics of verifier-guided search across coding and scientific optimization. Current evidence is one author-run preprint with heterogeneous baselines, limited repeated trials and execution failures that confound reward; consequence is major but conditional.
limitations: Baseline protocols, candidate budgets, hardware, and score aggregation differ across tasks; headline comparisons are not uniformly matched.
AHC058 reports a single official submission score rather than repeated-run means; TriMul timing is configuration-specific and compares selected eligible Triton entries.
Key model-scale comparisons have one trajectory, leaving search randomness as an alternative explanation.
Verifier reward combines strategic proposal quality with executor implementation validity; invalid candidates can receive zero reward even when the guidance idea is useful.
A separate 58% service-cost result compares one Polyomino configuration and does not establish general economics.
No independent reproduction was performed; linked GitHub run-manifest retrieval failed in this bounded review, and external hash-bound payloads remain unaudited.
summary: A 5 October 2026 preprint proposes Guidance-TTT, which updates a compact 8B or 14B model to suggest high-level changes while a stronger GLM-5.2 executor remains frozen and implements each proposal as a complete candidate. An executable verifier scores candidates; an archive and PUCT selection supply parents for later attempts. Authors report results on Polyomino Packing, Lasso path optimization, AHC058 and TriMul, including 91.89 on Polyomino, 0.1739 on Lasso, an AHC058 score of 850,082,731, and 1,129 μs TriMul latency. These are author-reported outcomes against heterogeneous prior references, not matched replications. Key model-scale comparisons use one trajectory, implementation failures affect verifier rewards, and full code/data artifacts have not been independently audited here.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report stronger results than selected prior references across four tasks and a configuration-specific reduction in service cost when adapting an 8B guide rather than a 120B solution model. The cost comparison is one Polyomino configuration and does not establish general compute economics.
technical.compute_or_cost: One separate Polyomino comparison reports about 58% lower service cost for adapting 8B guidance with GPT-OSS-120B execution than adapting the 120B model, at scores 83.19 and 83.72; this is configuration-specific. Attempt counts and full candidate/API/GPU budgets are not consistently matched to all baselines.
technical.demonstrated_result: The authors report 91.89 on Polyomino Packing, 0.1739 on Lasso, 850,082,731 on an AHC058 submission and 1,129 μs geometric-mean latency on TriMul. Main runs use 30 updates, 8 parent groups and 16 rollouts per group. Baselines vary by task and are often prior-work results rather than matched same-budget runs.
technical.implementation_status: Preprint links a public project/implementation; this activation did not fetch the full run manifest, execute code or independently verify remote artifact hashes.
technical.mechanism: A compact guidance model receives a selected parent solution, its summaries and verifier score, proposes a high-level natural-language change, and a frozen stronger executor implements that change into a full candidate. An executable verifier scores the candidate; a parent-linked archive and PUCT selection guide later attempts. Only the compact guidance policy is updated from grouped verifier feedback.
technical.novelty: Apply test-time RL to high-level parent-conditioned strategic edits while a stronger frozen model implements full solutions, separating guidance learning from code-generation adaptation.
technical.regime: Offline verifier-guided search without web access on Polyomino packing, Lasso path optimization, AHC058 production planning and TriMul GPU-kernel optimization. Qwen3-8B or Qwen3-14B guidance is adapted while GLM-5.2 remains frozen. Several headline references are not same-budget or repeated-seed comparisons.
technical.reproducibility: The paper reports setup and ablations, but there is one trajectory for key model-scale comparisons, full external payloads were not recovered, and no independent reproduction was performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: Task-specific published references including CORAL, TTT-Discover, OpenEvolve, SimpleTES and public eligible Triton leaderboard entries. Their protocols, budgets, hardware and result aggregation are heterogeneous; matched frozen-guidance ablations on Polyomino and TriMul are the most relevant internal controls.

title: Guidance-TTT trains a compact strategic guide while keeping the solution executor frozen
why_it_matters: Separating strategic proposals from full solution implementation could reduce the cost and credit-assignment burden of test-time search: a small model learns which change to try while a stronger fixed model handles implementation. The reported results span four coding/scientific optimization tasks, but mixed baselines, single-trajectory scaling results and invalid executable candidates leave the generality and economics unresolved.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across five evaluated VLMs and three repurposed safety domains, authors report lower refusal when matched harmful visual requests ask for a point or box than when they ask for a text answer.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The 15,401 matched pairs comprise 659 VLSU, 14,578 BBQ-V and 164 Asimov-2.0 items; one Gemini 3.5 Flash LLM judge scores refusal/compliance.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Authors report a fine-tuning recipe improves grounding refusal on Qwen3-VL-8B and VisionReasoner-7B while separately measuring benign over-refusal and PointArena capability.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The paper does not establish real-world harmful-action incidence or broad deployment prevalence.

evidence_gaps.description: The matched output-mode gap and proposed fine-tuning mitigation have not been independently replicated with human-validated labels and multiple judges.
The benchmark results do not measure real downstream harmful actions or general prevalence.

importance_rationale: If the reported output-mode gap generalizes to interfaces that act on model coordinates, text-only safety tests may materially overstate protection for VLM outputs consumed by agents or robots. Current evidence is one author-reported preprint across five models and three repurposed datasets, with a single LLM judge, a highly imbalanced dataset mix and no measured real-world incident rate; consequence is major but conditional.
limitations: Results are author-reported in one preprint and scored by a single LLM judge; no independent replication was recovered.
The dataset mix is highly imbalanced: BBQ-V contributes 14,578 of 15,401 matched pairs, while VLSU contributes 659 and Asimov-2.0 contributes 164.
Only five models are evaluated and fine-tuning results cover two open models.
Code and checkpoints were not available for this review; authors say code will follow acceptance.
No real-world incidence, downstream agent action or robot outcome is measured.
Repurposed benchmark prompts and model-native output templates may affect results; the study does not settle transfer across models or deployment settings.
summary: A 5 October 2026 preprint evaluates five vision-language models on 15,401 matched harmful visual requests, varying whether each request asks for a text answer or a spatial grounding such as a point or box. The authors report that grounding refusal trails text-answer refusal by 31–59 percentage points depending on the domain, and that safety system prompts do not close the gap. A fine-tuning recipe combining grounding-form refusals, capability data and benign examples reportedly improves refusal on two open models while tracking over-refusal and grounding capability. This is a single author-run preprint scored by one LLM judge; 14,578 of 15,401 pairs are from the social-bias dataset, code is not released, and real-world harm incidence is not established.

technical.claimed_result: The authors interpret the difference as a response-mode generalization gap and report that a training mixture improves grounding and text refusal on two open models. The paper does not establish real-world harm incidence or downstream action outcomes.
technical.compute_or_cost: No deployment cost or real-world incident-rate estimate is reported.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper reports 15,401 matched harmful pairs across VLSU (659), BBQ-V (14,578) and Asimov-2.0 (164), evaluated on five VLMs. Averaged grounding refusal trails VQA refusal by 31–59 percentage points depending on domain; system prompting does not close the gap. For Qwen3-VL-8B and VisionReasoner-7B, authors report fine-tuning gains in grounding refusal, including on held-out Asimov-2.0, while tracking PointArena capability and benign over-refusal.
technical.implementation_status: Public preprint; authors state code will be released upon acceptance. No code was run in this activation.
technical.mechanism: The authors convert three visual safety datasets into matched pairs that hold image, harmful intent and wording constant while changing only response mode: text VQA versus a native point or bounding-box grounding interface. A Gemini 3.5 Flash LLM judge scores refusal/compliance. Their fine-tuning combines grounding-form refusals, self-distilled benign examples and capability grounding data.
technical.novelty: Matched evaluation of whether refusal behavior transfers from text answers to spatial grounding outputs, with separate measurements for harmful refusal, benign over-refusal and grounding capability.
technical.regime: Five VLMs, three repurposed datasets and one Gemini 3.5 Flash LLM judge. The largest dataset is BBQ-V (14,578 of 15,401 matched pairs). Fine-tuning results cover Qwen3-VL-8B and VisionReasoner-7B. Benchmarks do not measure real-world harm or downstream action incidence.
technical.reproducibility: Author-reported v1 preprint; one LLM judge; code not yet released; no independent reproduction.
technical.strongest_baseline: Matched VQA-mode requests using the same image and harmful intent; for training, each model’s own pre-fine-tuning behavior. The paper also compares prompting and reports it does not close the gap, with some benign over-refusal trade-offs.

title: Preprint reports a visual-grounding refusal gap across five vision-language models
why_it_matters: When a model’s coordinates are consumed by a GUI agent or robot, a refusal policy that works for text may not carry over to the actionable spatial output. The paper motivates evaluating matched response modes and tracking safety alongside benign over-refusal and grounding capability. Its results do not establish deployment prevalence or real-world harm; the dataset mix, one-judge evaluation and small model sample need independent testing.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors propose a four-level, read-only hierarchy over one demonstration per base task, with clips retrieved as the planner reaches relevant subgoals.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In author-reported simulation results, HarnessVLA success rises from 92.6% to 96.5% on LIBERO-PRO and from 86.7% to 95.8% on LIBERO-Plus.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: LIBERO-PRO compares 50 RV-ICL episodes per cell with 100 prior-work baseline episodes; LIBERO-Plus evaluates a stratified 120 of 10,030 variants, with 17–18 cases per perturbation dimension.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The paper reports 1.8x wall-clock time and 1.4x input tokens versus HarnessVLA on the LIBERO-Plus subset; all experiments are in simulation and use one robot and one VLA.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The reported improvement does not establish transfer to physical robots or broad task distributions, and the main LIBERO-PRO baseline comparison is not matched episode by episode.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent matched-seed replication or recovered per-episode RV-ICL results and exact seed list; the paper’s aggregate significance statistic is not independently auditable.
Physical-robot transfer and performance across other VLA models, robots and task families remain unknown.

importance_rationale: If the reported improvement transfers under matched trials, retrieving demonstration video only at relevant subgoals could materially improve long-horizon manipulation without retraining the VLA. The evidence is one author-reported simulation paper with unequal sample counts for its main baseline comparison, small perturbation cells and a latency/token cost, so the consequence is notable but conditional.
limitations: The main LIBERO-PRO baseline values are reported from prior work with 100 episodes per cell; RV-ICL uses 50, so the comparison is not same-run or episode-matched.

Authors report z=2.97, p=0.003 for the aggregate LIBERO-PRO comparison, but exact per-task/seed outcomes, seed overlap and test code were not recovered; aggregate-count recomputation and dependence handling remain open.
LIBERO-Plus uses a stratified 120 of 10,030 variants, with only 17–18 examples per perturbation dimension.
The reported LIBERO-Plus success change costs 1.8x wall-clock time and 1.4x input tokens relative to HarnessVLA.
All experiments are simulated, use one robot and one VLA, and do not establish performance on physical robots or other embodiments.
Demonstrations are assumed to expose task sub-events; tasks lacking gripper/fixture event signals need other segmentation methods.
summary: A 5 October 2026 preprint reports Recursive Video In-Context Learning (RV-ICL), which indexes one task demonstration into four read-only levels—keyframes, phases, moments and short clips—and lets a planner retrieve detail for its current subgoal. The authors report HarnessVLA success rising from 92.6% to 96.5% on LIBERO-PRO and 86.7% to 95.8% on LIBERO-Plus. These are author-reported simulation results: on LIBERO-PRO the RV-ICL arm used 50 episodes while prior-work baselines used 100, and the paper’s reported significance statistic does not yet have a recovered matched-data audit. On LIBERO-Plus the methods were compared on a stratified 120 of 10,030 variants. The paper reports 1.8x wall-clock time and 1.4x input tokens on that comparison; physical-robot transfer is untested.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report that recursive, subgoal-specific video retrieval improves a frozen-VLA agent across perturbed simulation benchmarks and carries to a second planner. No independent replication or physical-robot outcome was established.
technical.compute_or_cost: On the LIBERO-Plus subset, authors report 1.8x wall-clock time and 1.4x input tokens versus HarnessVLA. Video preparation/storage and deployment economics were not established.
technical.demonstrated_result: The authors report HarnessVLA success increasing from 92.6% to 96.5% on LIBERO-PRO and 86.7% to 95.8% on LIBERO-Plus. LIBERO-PRO RV-ICL results aggregate 50 episodes per cell versus 100 for prior-work baselines. LIBERO-Plus uses a stratified subset of 120 from 10,030 variants, with 17–18 cases per perturbation dimension. The paper reports 1.8x wall-clock time and 1.4x input tokens versus HarnessVLA on the LIBERO-Plus subset.
technical.implementation_status: Authors link a public code repository and describe a runnable pipeline; the research desk did not run or independently audit it in this activation.
technical.mechanism: RV-ICL segments one demonstration per base task at task sub-events and exposes a four-level hierarchy—event keyframes, phases, moments and short video clips—through read-only tools. The planner first reads coarse levels and can retrieve a clip for the current subgoal during execution, subject to a viewing budget.
technical.novelty: Treat a demonstration as a hierarchical, queryable memory that the planner revisits when a subgoal needs visual detail, rather than providing the full video or fixed keyframes up front.
technical.regime: One demonstration per base task; GPT-6 Astra planner orchestrating a frozen pi0.5 primitive through RPent/HarnessVLA; LIBERO-PRO and a stratified LIBERO-Plus simulation subset. No other robot embodiment, physical deployment or broad task distribution was evaluated.
technical.reproducibility: Paper reports its sample counts and configurations, but exact per-episode outcomes, exact seed IDs and statistical code were not recovered. The main LIBERO-PRO comparison uses a prior-work baseline with a different episode count.
technical.strongest_baseline: HarnessVLA with the same frozen pi0.5 primitive. On LIBERO-PRO, the baseline values are from prior work and use twice as many episodes per cell; on the paper’s stratified LIBERO-Plus subset, the authors run both methods in the same time window.

title: Recursive video retrieval reports higher frozen-VLA success on perturbed simulation tasks
why_it_matters: The hierarchy makes demonstration video an on-demand memory source: an agent sees task structure before planning and retrieves short clips near a grasp, release or other subgoal. If the reported gains survive matched testing, this could improve long-horizon manipulation without retraining the VLA. Current evidence is limited to one author-run simulation study with unequal LIBERO-PRO sample counts, small perturbation cells and a measurable latency/token cost.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: ECB staff report lower leverage among high-AI sectors, especially developers, and a recent shift toward market-based debt financing among high adopters.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The staff blog reports sector debt-financing growth observations through April 2026 and leverage observations through 2025Q3.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The ECB staff BVAR through 2024Q4 reports a stronger peak credit and investment response to an AI-patent-share shock in the US than in the euro area.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Deeper US capital markets are offered as one possible explanation, not established as the causal mechanism.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The patent-share/instrument comparison predates the October blog in Philip Lane’s March 2026 speech; the October item is a staff analysis update, not independent confirmation.

evidence_gaps.description: The BVAR instrument, priors, sector coding and sensitivity results have not been independently audited or reproduced.
The proposed capital-market explanation is not identified as causal, and aggregate results do not establish firm-level effects.

importance_rationale: If the reported financing shift and cross-region response difference are robust, capital-market structure could materially shape AI investment and its sensitivity to monetary conditions. The findings come from ECB staff analysis using sector classifications and an internal-instrument BVAR; they do not establish causal mechanisms or firm-level effects.
limitations: ECB blog authors state that their views do not necessarily represent the ECB or Eurosystem.
The patent-share internal instrument is a proxy for AI-related expectations/news and does not directly measure AI adoption, firm productivity or causal capital-market effects.
Sector classifications use top/bottom adoption and development quartiles based on 2023–25 data; AI patent taxonomies omit unpatented innovation and are classification-dependent.
The BVAR ends in 2024Q4, while balance-sheet debt-financing observations extend through April 2026; these are distinct data windows.
No code, technical appendix, prior/sensitivity table or independent reproduction was recovered.
Sector aggregates do not establish financing behavior or outcomes for individual firms.
summary: In an ECB staff blog dated 6 October 2026, authors classify euro-area sectors by AI adoption using Eurostat enterprise surveys and by AI development using patent shares. Sectoral balance-sheet data through April 2026 show high-AI sectors, especially developers, with lower leverage and a recent shift toward market-based debt financing. A quarterly Bayesian VAR through 2024Q4 reports a stronger peak credit and investment response to an AI-patent-share shock in the United States than in the euro area. The authors suggest deeper US capital markets as one possible explanation; this is staff analysis, not an ECB Governing Council position or an independently reproduced causal estimate.

technical.claimed_result: The authors suggest deeper US venture-capital, equity and unified markets may help explain the stronger US response. They explicitly present this as one possible explanation; the reported design does not by itself identify that mechanism as causal.
technical.compute_or_cost: Not applicable; no compute-cost estimate is reported.
technical.demonstrated_result: The official ECB blog reports that high-AI sectors, particularly AI developers, have lower sector-median leverage and that high adopters have recently shifted debt financing toward market-based instruments. Latest observations are Q3 2025 for leverage and April 2026 for debt-financing growth. The BVAR sample runs 1999Q1–2024Q4 and reports stronger peak credit and investment responses to the calibrated AI-patent-share shock in the US than in the euro area.
technical.implementation_status: ECB staff blog analysis, publicly available; not an ECB Governing Council decision.
technical.mechanism: The authors classify euro-area sectors by AI adoption from Eurostat ICT enterprise surveys and AI development from AI-related patent shares. They combine sectoral firm balance-sheet data with quarterly Bayesian VARs using the share of AI patents among total patents as an internal instrument for AI-related news.
technical.novelty: Updated sectoral debt-financing evidence through April 2026 and an explicit adoption-versus-development classification alongside an earlier ECB patent-news BVAR comparison.
technical.regime: Euro-area sector-level financing classifications and quarterly US/euro-area BVAR estimates; sector AI adoption is based on survey data and development on patent shares. Do not generalize the aggregate estimates to individual firms or infer a causal effect of capital-market depth.
technical.reproducibility: No code, technical appendix, priors/sensitivity tables or independent estimate audit was recovered in this bounded review.
technical.strongest_baseline: The same ECB authors’ earlier 23 March 2026 speech presented an AI-patent-share internal-instrument BVAR comparison through 2024Q4. The October blog extends sector financing observations through April 2026 and separates AI adopters from developers; this is an update, not independent replication.

title: ECB staff analysis reports AI-intensive euro-area sectors shifting toward market-based debt finance
why_it_matters: Financing structure can shape how AI investment responds to interest rates and how quickly firms scale. The reported shift toward market-based debt and the cross-region difference motivate closer measurement of AI-sector financing and capital-market depth. The BVAR result is a model-based response to a patent-share instrument, not proof that capital-market structure causes the difference or that firm-level AI investment has a particular return.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report a Lean 4 formalization of global Leray–Hopf weak-solution existence for unforced 2D Navier–Stokes on arbitrary bounded open domains with no-slip boundaries.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper also reports a finite-horizon forced weak-solution formalization on rectangles under its stated admissible-forcing assumptions.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The linked public repository README identifies PDEIdeas.Paper as the entry point and documents `lake exe cache get` followed by `lake build`; successful independent compilation was not established here.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED

summary: Potraghloo and colleagues present on-policy power distillation (OPPD), which uses sequential Monte Carlo samples from the model being trained and a frozen teacher’s sharpened sequence distribution to reweight a maximum-likelihood update. The authors report single-generation accuracy increases of up to 23.0 points on MATH500 and 27.3 points on GSM8K over the untrained model at the same temperature, and report gains in a same-checkpoint GRPO comparison. Their abstract also claims performance above published 64-candidate power-sampling results; the existing candidate review found that this comparison uses a different evaluation protocol, while the same-paper 16-candidate comparison is close and does not show OPPD ahead. These are author-reported preprint outcomes, not independent validation or a matched total training-plus-inference cost result.

summary: Jaffe and Sherburn introduce TasteVal, an author-built benchmark of eight text and vision tasks intended to measure experimental design and interpretation when a fixed research problem is given. They report that Opus 5.5 (max) reaches a 2.30× experimental-compute multiplier against the best expert attempt per task (95% CI 1.15–4.37). The authors also estimate that frontier-model multiplier performance doubled about every 3.0 months after December 2025, while final normalized performance shows no corresponding trend break. These are preprint results on withheld tasks, not evidence that models choose valuable research questions or outperform experts across broad research work.

The 2.30× benchmark metric is serial experimental compute; forecast extrapolations assume, without established transfer, that the measured rate applies to broader frontier AI R&D.

summary: Gao and colleagues study how four language models count repeated reports across controlled sensor logs with an exact Bayesian oracle, web documents, and generated multi-agent transcripts. Their abstract reports that a forwarded copy counts as 0.06–0.42 of an independent reading, and that repeated statements can imply premature commitment on 5%–40% of logs in the tested settings. The authors report that a declaration about copy contribution lowers copy weight to 0.08 or less on controlled logs, while a worker-side rule to refer to readings rather than restate them lowers belief-implied early commitment from 11.2% to 1.1% in their team-log protocol. This is one author-reported preprint, not an operational error rate or independent replication.

summary: Yang and Wang report testing 14 models on 30 pairs of mechanics problems, each with a valid version and a version made impossible by changing an input or assumption. A later retest found that warning/status prompts raised rejection for three of four models but lowered valid-problem solving for three. summary: On 2026-09-14, China’s National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity (TC260), under CAC guidance, published the Chinese-language AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0. Its 136-page document classifies risks and recommends mitigations across AI-agent design, installation/deployment, instruction input, reasoning/planning, tool execution, memory, output and shutdown. It identifies prompt injection, context overflow, tool poisoning and overreach, memory contamination/theft, behavior escape, and residual credentials/processes after shutdown. Recommended controls include pre-deployment risk assessment, staged increases in access and autonomy, unique agent identity and least privilege, revocable credentials, human approval and ability to interrupt high-risk operations, fail-closed approval handling, runtime guardrails, and memory isolation. Comparison with the official 2025 Framework 2.0 shows that 2.0 already discussed autonomous agent planning and privilege/file-access risks, but did not have a dedicated agentic-AI lifecycle appendix. Version 3.0 adds that appendix and separately maps agent identity/permission, planning, tool-execution, memory, embodied and multi-agent risks. This documents a change in framework scope; neither publication establishes binding law, broad adoption or control effectiveness.

technical.claimed_result: The release describes the framework as updating risk classifications and optimizing technical response and comprehensive governance measures to improve shared understanding and risk response. These are the issuing body's stated aims, not measured outcomes.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary document contains a structured agent risk taxonomy and these control recommendations (Chinese PDF pp.37–48; PDF pages 41–52 in the web-rendered file, with specific text at lines 981–1137). This demonstrates what the framework recommends, not that any system implements or benefits from the controls.
technical.implementation_status: TC260 announced Framework 3.0 on 2026-09-14. The official 136-page bilingual 3.0 PDF and official 92-page bilingual 2.0 PDF were both text-inspected for this targeted comparison. No implementation audit was attempted.
technical.mechanism: The document treats agent security as a lifecycle problem and recommends layered controls: pre-use risk review; incremental increases in access/autonomy; unique identities and least privilege; revocable credentials; safety checks on tools, skills and their metadata; human approval and interruptibility at high-risk decision points; runtime monitoring and fail-closed handling; segmented memory with limited retention; and cleanup/revocation when the agent is retired.
technical.regime: Chinese-language national cybersecurity technical guidance for AI R&D, deployment and use, including agentic systems; applicability, legal force and adoption by organizations are not established by the inspected release materials.
technical.reproducibility: Not an experimental result. The claims about document content are directly inspectable in the primary PDF; adoption and control effectiveness require separate evidence.
technical.strongest_baseline: The official 2025 Framework 2.0 already mentions autonomous agent planning, access to files/permissions/interfaces/tools, privilege abuse, application risk grading and an agent glossary definition. Framework 3.0 adds a dedicated Agentic AI risk-management appendix and explicit categories for identity/permission, planning, invocation/execution, memory, embodied and multi-agent risks.

why_it_matters: The framework translates agent security concerns into a lifecycle control set spanning identity, permissions, tool supply chains, untrusted inputs, long-term memory, human intervention and shutdown. If implemented, these recommendations could change agent platform architecture and deployment review. The consequence is bounded because this is a guidance document and no adoption, enforcement, or control effectiveness was established.

summary: On 6 October 2026, the UK government published its response to the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare and accepted all 44 recommendations. It sets a one-year delivery focus on proportionate lifecycle regulation, post-market assurance, system readiness, transparency and predictable regulatory pathways. The MHRA says it intends to issue draft guidance on Predetermined Change Control Plans by December 2026 and launch a consultation on device qualification and classification by Spring 2027; most other timelines are also due by Spring 2027. The MHRA opened applications for AI Airlock Phase 3, focused on post-market surveillance and lifecycle regulation, funded through April 2029. The programme charges no application or participation fee, but selected candidates are expected to pay for their own studies, testing work and relevant data access; each bespoke engagement is generally scoped for 6–12 months. This is a government commitment and sandbox launch, not enactment of new statutory requirements or evidence of improved patient outcomes.

technical.claimed_result: The government says the package is intended to support safe, effective and scalable healthcare AI adoption, patient safety, transparency and innovation. Those effects remain expected outcomes, not measured results.
technical.compute_or_cost: The inspected application notice provides no total programme budget, grant to participating teams, per-project allocation, compliance-cost estimate or expected health-system savings. There is no application or participation fee, but candidates are expected to fund their own studies, testing delivery and relevant data access; bespoke engagement is generally 6–12 months. Phase 3 is funded through April 2029.
technical.demonstrated_result: The official response states that government accepts all 44 Commission recommendations. It specifies a draft PCCP guidance target of December 2026 and a consultation on qualification/classification by Spring 2027. AI Airlock Phase 3 applications opened on 6 October and Phase 3 is funded through April 2029. The application notice states that applying and participating carry no fee, but selected candidates are expected to fund their studies, testing and relevant data access, with individual plans generally scoped to 6–12 months. These are documented programme terms, not evidence that the planned requirements or outcomes have been delivered.
technical.implementation_status: Government response published October 6, 2026. All 44 recommendations accepted. AI Airlock Phase 3 opened for applications; first cohort selection is planned for November 2026. Consultation and guidance milestones are scheduled into December 2026 and Spring 2027.
technical.mechanism: The response assigns MHRA, DHSC, NHS England and devolved partners work on risk-based device qualification/classification, lifecycle evidence, PCCPs, model dependency disclosure, strengthened post-market surveillance, patient transparency and system readiness. AI Airlock Phase 3 gives eligible developers and regulators a sandbox to investigate post-market surveillance practices with real products.
technical.novelty: Moves the September Commission recommendations from advisory proposals to accepted cross-government commitments, while immediately launching a sandbox phase focused on post-market surveillance.
technical.regime: United Kingdom regulation and deployment of software and AI-enabled medical devices across the healthcare system; scope includes device manufacturers, general-purpose-model dependencies, NHS providers and devolved health partners.
technical.reproducibility: The policy status and listed milestones are directly checkable in the published government response. Implementation progress and downstream effects require later monitoring.
technical.strongest_baseline: The September 10, 2026 National Commission report was an independent, non-statutory advisory set of recommendations. The October 6 government response changes their status to accepted government commitments while leaving most implementation details and any legislative reform to future work.

title: UK government accepts all 44 recommendations on AI healthcare regulation and opens AI Airlock Phase 3
why_it_matters: If implemented, the response could materially change evidence, version-control, post-market monitoring and market-entry expectations for AI-enabled medical devices across the UK, including products built on general-purpose models. The near-term consequence is a clearer implementation direction and a testing channel funded through April 2029. Participation is free, but applicants bear study, testing and data-access costs, so the programme does not itself establish that smaller developers face lower deployment costs. Most requirements remain future work, and economic or safety effects are not yet demonstrated.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Lei 15.504/2026 establishes Redata for projects installing, modernizing or expanding data-center services in Brazil; the statutory definition expressly includes cloud, high-performance computing and AI model training and inference.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: To qualify, applicants commit to make at least 10% of the effective processing, storage and data-treatment supply installed with Redata benefits available to the domestic market. The statute measures domestic allocation using annual gross revenue from domestic-market services divided by total gross revenue from the benefited services; free transfers to eligible ICTs or public bodies may count using a regulatory multiplier, and the 10% availability commitment may instead be replaced by an additional 10% investment in eligible R&D. Applicants must also meet sustainability rules; supply all contracted electricity from renewable or low-emission generation via contracts or self-production; report annual cooling WUE no higher than 0.05 L/kWh; and invest 2% of benefited ICT-product purchases in eligible Brazilian digital-economy R&D. Certain local-service and R&D commitments are reduced by 20% for facilities in the North, Northeast and Center-West.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED

summary: Brazil's Lei 15.504/2026 creates Redata, a five-year tax-incentive regime for qualifying data-center installation, modernization and expansion, including AI training and inference. Applicants must make at least 10% of the effective processing, storage and data-treatment supply installed with Redata benefits available to Brazil's domestic market; the law calculates that commitment using domestic gross revenue as a share of total gross revenue from the benefited services, with implementation details left to regulation. Applicants must also meet renewable or low-emission electricity and sustainability requirements, keep cooling WUE at or below 0.05 L/kWh, and invest 2% of incentivized ICT-product purchases in local digital-economy R&D. The law suspends specified taxes on eligible ICT equipment; PIS/Pasep, Cofins and IPI provisions currently run through 2026-12-31 under the tax-transition clause. A separate complementary law, LC 237/2026, also places Redata within specified 2026 exceptions to tax-benefit restrictions, subject to primary-balance and annual-budget conditions, and requires MDIC and the Ministry of Finance to monitor and evaluate the benefits against their objectives.

technical.claimed_result: The government describes Redata as a way to attract data-center investment, strengthen digital sovereignty and support low-carbon development.
technical.compute_or_cost: The law creates specified tax suspensions; actual savings, tax expenditure, equipment uptake and facility costs have not been measured.
technical.demonstrated_result: Enacted eligibility, tax terms and conditional commitments for Brazilian data-center projects, including AI training and inference.
technical.implementation_status: Lei 15.504/2026 entered into force on publication on 2026-09-15; eligibility and co-eligibility procedures, qualifying goods and several sustainability/accounting details require executive regulation. Lei Complementar 237/2026 (2026-09-15) adds Redata to specified exceptions from 2026 tax-benefit restrictions, conditional on primary-balance compatibility and annual-budget inclusion, and requires MDIC and the Ministry of Finance to monitor and evaluate the benefits against stated objectives.
technical.mechanism: Federal Revenue habilitation links tax suspension on qualifying ICT fixed assets to domestic service availability, eligible energy sourcing, water-efficiency, sustainability and R&D commitments; the domestic-service commitment is measured by domestic gross revenue share, and failure can trigger tax recovery, penalties or loss of authorization.
technical.novelty: An investment tax regime for data centers directly conditions equipment-tax relief on local compute availability and quantified energy, water and R&D obligations.
technical.regime: Brazilian data-center installation, modernization or expansion; statute covers cloud, HPC and AI training/inference. Five-year duration subject to tax-transition clauses and implementing regulations.
technical.reproducibility: Binding statute is publicly available; implementation and realized outcomes remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: The new statute formalizes a dedicated Redata regime rather than generic data-center incentives; its commitments and qualifying equipment lists depend on regulation.

title: Brazil ties data-center tax relief to clean power, local capacity and R&D commitments
why_it_matters: The regime trades conditional import and equipment-tax relief for domestic compute availability, clean-energy sourcing, water efficiency and local innovation spending. These terms can affect data-center location and project economics, but actual tax expenditure, approvals, construction and compliance outcomes remain unmeasured. LC 237/2026 defines Redata’s treatment under specified 2026 tax-benefit controls and creates a statutory monitoring/evaluation duty, while preserving primary-balance and budget conditions; neither provision establishes actual tax expenditure or impact.
